previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with Type 1 diabetes, gastroparesis s/p gastric pacer, and hypertension was admitted for intractable nausea and vomiting. She developed respiratory depression after receiving 1 mg IV Ativan in the ED, requiring ICU monitoring, but recovered within 24 hours. She also experienced hypertensive urgency with BP up to 215/140, managed with IV labetalol and hydralazine, and presented with a single episode of hematemesis likely due to a Mallory-Weiss tear, prompting temporary discontinuation of aspirin and initiation of twice-daily PPI therapy. Her blood glucose was elevated on admission, raising concern for DKA, but was managed with increased insulin coverage without needing an insulin drip. She was treated with IV fluids, antiemetics including ondansetron, Reglan, and IV erythromycin, and advanced to a regular diet. She was discharged home in stable condition tolerating oral intake, with instructions to avoid high-dose benzodiazepines, follow up with GI for pacer interrogation and erythromycin evaluation, and continue home medications including adjusted lisinopril and insulin regimen.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ yo woman with DM Type I and gastroparesis s/p gastric pacer 
___, presents with nausea and vomiting. 

1. Gastroparesis: The patient's severe nausea and vomiting were 
thought to be secondary to her gastroparesis. She has had 
multiple admissions over the past 3 months for poor PO intake 
for this same reason.  She was put on a diet of clears while 
hospitalized and advanced as tolerated. She was kept on IV 
fluids for rehydration, except for when she had developed 
hyponatremia, which was thought to be secondary to an SIADH she 
commonly develops when hospitalized for nausea/vomiting.  She 
was seen by gastroenterology, who performed an upper endoscopy 
to determine if there was an additional source of her symptoms 
other than gastroparesis.  No such source was found.  Endoscopy 
showed esophagitis, and biopsy confirmed this.  There were no 
abnomalities of the stomach mucosa.  One day prior to discharge, 
her gastric pacer was readjusted.  Following this procedure, her 
nausea and vomiting improved and she was tolerating solid foods. 
 She was discharged on ___ and instructed to follow up with 
her gastroenterologist, Dr. ___ next day.  She was 
discharged on erythromycin, reglan, zofran, and compazine. 

2. Hypertension:  The patient was on a home dose of lisinopril 
7.5mg daily and a clonidine patch before admission.  While 
hospitalized, she was unable to tolerate her oral medications 
and she consistently had 160's-170's SBP. She was started on 
labetalol 10mg IV q6h until she was able to tolerate her PO 
meds.  Her blood pressures were still 140's to 150's systolic on 
lisinopril 7.5mg and her clonidine patch.  Her lisinopril was 
increased to 10mg daily and her clonidine patch was ultimately 
discontinued as one of the major side effects is nausea.  She 
will follow up with her PCP next week and hypertensive 
medications changes can be discussed at that time.  She was give 
a prescription to have a chem-7 drawn before her appointment 
given the increased dose of ACEi.

3. Hyponatremia:  While hospitalized, the patient had a sodium 
as low as 128.  It was felt to be secondary to SIADH from her 
extreme nausea and vomiting.  She was fluid restricted and IV 
fluids were held.  Sodium level gradually rose to 134 upon 
discharge.

4. Leukocytosis:  The patient had a leukocytosis up to 12.2 
during hospitalization.  This was felt to be secondary to a 
stress response, but since the patient was tachycardic and had a 
temperature of 95.6, she met SIRS criteria and blood and urine 
cultures were drawn.  Her vital signs and WBC eventually 
normalized when the nausea and vomiting resolved.  Her blood and 
urine cultures were negative for growth.

5. Diabetes Mellitus, type 1:  Upon admission, the patient was 
on lantus 28 units QHS with a sliding scale. When she was not 
tolerating anything by mouth, she was given half her lantus dose 
and otherwise managed with the sliding scale.  When discharged, 
she was instructed to maintain her home regimen of lantus 28 
units QHS with sliding scale.

6. Anemia: At baseline Hct, patient for colonoscopy later this 
year.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital with nausea/vomiting and 
dehydration.  This was due to your gastroparesis. While you were 
in the hospital, you were given IV fluids because you weren't 
able to tolerate anything by mouth. 

While you were in the hospital, your sodium level was low. We 
put you on a fluid restriction, which normalized your sodium 
levels. We did a Chest Xray to make sure there was nothing in 
your lungs to cause this low sodium. The chest XRay was 
negative. It was most likely a response to your severe nausea.

You were also taking a number of anti-nausea medications while 
you were here through the IV. Now that you are tolerating a 
diet, you can take your nausea medications by mouth. You can 
resume the same regimen you were on before coming to the 
hospital. Your gastric pacer was readjusted by Dr. ___ 
you were in the hospital. You have an appointment with him 
tomorrow for follow up.

You were also taken for an endoscopy while you were in the 
hospital. You were found to have severe esophagitis 
(inflammation of your esophagus).  You should continue to take 
pantoprazole as an outpatient for this, as you are prescribed.  
No additional cause for your nausea and vomiting was found.

While you were in the hospital, your blood pressure was very 
high. We had to give you medications through the IV because you 
couldn't take your blood pressure medications by mouth.  You 
should follow up with Dr. ___ PCP, about blood pressure 
control as an outpatient, as it was high when you were here in 
the hospital. Your clonidine patch was discontinued while you 
were in the hospital because we thought it might be contributing 
to your nausea.

We have increased your lisinopril dose to 10mg a day for blood 
pressure control. Take two 5mg tablets once a day. You are being 
given a prescription for a blood test to be drawn before you see 
your primary care physician.  This is to monitor your potassium 
on this increased dose of lisinopril.

You have an appointment with Dr. ___ gastroenterologist 
tomorrow. He made changes to your gastric pacer on ___.

Please return to the ER or call your doctor if you have nausea 
and vomiting to the extent that you cannot tolerate anything by 
mouth.  Also return if you are feeling dizzy, chest pains, 
shortness of breath, fever, chills, or any symptoms that are 
concerning to you.
